title: MODERN DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES FOR SUSTAINABLE TOURISM DEVELOPMENT IN GEORGIA
abstract: Tourism is one of the most important and rapidly developing sectors of the global economy, contributing significantly to economic growth, employment creation, cultural exchange, and the international positioning of countries. In the contemporary world, tourism has become closely interconnected with digital technologies, which have fundamentally transformed the ways in which tourism services are produced, promoted, and consumed. The present study explores the role of modern digital technologies in supporting sustainable tourism development in Georgia. It examines how digital transformation, including online platforms, mobile applications, social media, artificial intelligence, and digital marketing systems, influences tourist behavior and reshapes the tourism industry. Georgia possesses substantial tourism potential due to its rich cultural heritage, historical monuments, diverse landscapes, and unique geographical location. However, despite continuous growth in tourist arrivals, the country still faces structural and technological challenges that limit full utilization of its tourism resources. The paper analyzes both opportunities and challenges associated with digital tourism development, including globalization of tourism markets, increasing digital dependency of tourists, changes in consumer behavior, and issues such as digital inequality and lack of technological infrastructure. The study concludes that sustainable tourism development in Georgia is directly dependent on the effective integration of digital technologies, improved marketing strategies, and the strengthening of human capital in the tourism sector.

title: Unscrambling the Eggs: Automated Data Extraction from Structured Record Cards
abstract: The Natural History Museum in the UK (NHM) is home to more than 80 million objects spanning 4.5 billion years of history. Each of these contain a wealth of data, whether on specimen labels, index cards, registers and/or diaries. Transcribing and categorising this information can help unlock crucial research potential. To do this at scale, we turn to computer vision (CV) and Machine Learning (ML) techniques to automate this work. Over a million of the museum’s specimens are ornithological, including one of the largest and most comprehensive egg collections in the world. Representing 52% of known bird species, with over 300,000 clutches (where a clutch defines the total group of eggs laid in a nest), collected over the last 200 years, arguably make this the most important archive of avian environmental change data in existence(Norris et al. 2023). The eggs were historically catalogued using index cards, containing key information such as identification, collection date, locality and clutch size. A proportion of these egg cards have now been imaged and this led to the start of this project, focusing on a sample of 15,000 photographed egg cards (example seen in Fig. 1). Our initial approach used Google Vision to perform Optical Character Recognition (OCR) to transcribe all text with the egg cards. By focusing on textboxes around key terms (e.g., “Collector”), and using CV tools, we approximated boxes around every key category. Finally, each text segment was associated to a category box, followed by minor post-processing in order to extract (i.e., transcribe and categorise) the data. Here we successfully extracted the data within the sample, with a 98.6% average accuracy. Although our methods worked well for our sample, they did rely on consistency within the structures of cards. To expand the project further, and to mitigate the reliance on consistent structures within cards, we turned to Large Language Models (LLMs). This allowed us to explore automatic data extraction from different types of cards and labels, despite variation in the card structure, and even handle unknown categories of text. Consequently, the scope of the data collected was widened, such as adding ornithological specimen data (e.g., skins), as well as external datasets through collaboration with the British Trust for Ornithology, who manage the Nest Record Scheme (Crick et al. 2003), which holds decades of vital information on the progress of monitored nests in the UK. This index-card data-extraction project is just the beginning. As we expand our data extraction capabilities, our aim is to develop a novel pipeline that can be applied not just to avifauna-related cards, but any structured textual data, with the potential to unlock invaluable insights.

title: Investigating pre-Columbian floristic legacy effects using machine learning in the southern Atlantic Forest, Brazil
abstract: The scope and scale of past human impacts on both historic and current vegetation is of widespread interest in the historical sciences. In the Atlantic Forest of southern Brazil (Portuguese: Mata Atlântica), previous work has identified Amerindian settlement and land-use as a probable driver of the extent and composition of forest cover, with time-extended legacies that remain detectable in modern floristic inventories. Previously published investigations into the ecological history of the southern Atlantic Forest have either eschewed the role of humans or, where anthropogenic drivers are explicitly examined, utilized spatially restricted environmental datasets, necessarily limiting the generalizability their conclusions. This study aims to redress this gap, and to quantify the impact of past Amerindian Pre-Columbian settlement and associated land use on the modern-day distribution of several key plant species across the entire southern Atlantic Forest. We fit Maxent species distribution models (SDMs) using Indigenous archaeological site locations (Tupi-Guarani and southern Jê) and modern plant species occurrence data (35 unique species) in a comparative analytical framework to investigate Indigenous influence on the likelihood of occurrence of culturally significant or medicinal plant species. Our results indicate that (i) the inclusion of archaeological settlement location data and SDM predictions as covariates can improve the performance of contemporary floristic species distribution modeling and should be incorporated into ecological models of plant species in landscapes with long-standing human presence, especially when they are used to inform policy that explicitly aims to preserve “natural” biomes and; (ii) a synanthropic relationship can be demonstrated between the southern Jê and Araucaria angustifolia , a finding that complements previously published phylogeographic and palaeoenvironmental studies exploring the same link.

title: Editorial: Data analytics in sustainable city planning
abstract: Predictive analytics play an increasingly central role in sustainable city planning. By applying machine learning algorithms to large-scale and multi-source datasets, cities are able to forecast dynamic phenomena such as traffic congestion, crime incidents, and flood risk. These anticipatory insights are crucial for proactive urban management, allowing for early interventions and resource optimisation. Alongside this, the emergence of Digital Twins marks a shift from reactive to real-time urban governance. As a result, cities such as Singapore, Los Angeles, and Amsterdam improve these models to manage infrastructure across sectors including transportation, water supply, energy distribution, and public space usage. These digital ecosystems enable planners to test policy scenarios, monitor service performance, and respond adaptively to changing conditions.The integration of socio-demographic data into geospatial models enables researchers to identify and analyse disparities in urban vulnerability. For instance, spatial mapping of heat exposure in Indian cities such as Delhi and Bengaluru has informed the more equitable allocation of cooling infrastructure. These equity-oriented approaches ensure that sustainability initiatives are not only technically robust but also socially inclusive. Indeed, they support policymakers in targeting resources toward the most vulnerable populations and thereby addressing persistent inequalities in urban service delivery.The role of participatory digital platforms is a critical dimension of the sustainable planning discourse. Cities are increasingly turning to the use of GIS tools and e-planning applications to facilitate community involvement in the urban design process. These tools democratise access to data and decision-making and enable citizens to co-create solutions for their neighbourhoods. Such participation enhances the legitimacy and responsiveness of urban policy especially in contexts where historically marginalised groups have been excluded from formal planning mechanisms. Yet, these advances underscore the growing urgency of ethical data governance. As cities collect and analyse vast amounts of personal and behavioural data, questions of privacy, consent, and accountability become ever more noticeable. Past missteps, such as the lack of transparency in data-sharing partnerships in cities like Portland and Toronto, highlight the need for inclusive governance frameworks that safeguard public trust! One of the key contributions to this research topic comes from a comparative study of enduring smart city data platforms with a focus on the UK's Urban Observatories and the US Smart Columbus Operating System (Wolf et al.). The paper highlights the importance of long-term institutional commitment, interoperability, and public value in building resilient data infrastructures for urban management. Drawing from these two mature initiatives, the authors underscore the need for flexible data governance frameworks, sustained funding, and active community engagement to ensure data platforms not only serve immediate operational needs but evolve into lasting public assets. These lessons offer a strategic framework for future cities seeking to integrate data analytics into sustainable and inclusive urban development.In a complementary context, Hansen et al. analyse the evolution of Smart City initiatives in Thailand, highlighting the role of data in driving innovation, responsiveness, and inclusivity. Using platforms like Traffy Fondue (an application that enables citizens to report local issues in real time), the study shows how integrating environmental sensors, citizen feedback, and digital governance tools significantly improve municipal performance. Notably, the research underscores that these digital infrastructures also foster participatory governance by embedding residents more directly in decision-making processes. As Thailand's urban centres expand, these insights offer a replicable model for other emerging economies seeking to build dataliterate and community-centred smart cities. Xia et al. provide a comprehensive review of the relationship between urban renewal and sustainable public space development by highlighting key trends, obstacles, and future directions. It discusses how modern urban renewal increasingly incorporates sustainability through green infrastructure, adaptive reuse, and community-centric design, aiming to enhance liveability while preserving cultural heritage. Besides, this study emphasises the need for inclusive planning approaches that prioritise long-term ecological and social benefits, and offers insights into how cities can transform public spaces to foster resilience, equity, and environmental health in urban environments.In a more technical contribution, Xing et al. introduce a novel approach for assessing the physical disorder of architectural façades using deep learning and space syntax analysis. By processing street-level imagery through neural networks and evaluating spatial accessibility using syntactic metrics, the authors develop a multiscale index that can detect deterioration at the building, street, and city levels. This index enables urban planners to identify and prioritise areas in need of intervention, facilitating data-informed renewal strategies that enhance walkability and public perception. The study exemplifies how cutting-edge technologies are able to generate actionable insights for maintaining the integrity of urban environments.Taken collectively, this special issue signals several critical directions for the future of datainformed urban planning. A notable trend is the convergence of once-siloed smart city applications into comprehensive, multi-domain Digital Twins, made possible by advances in AI, IoT, and platform interoperability. There is also a growing shift toward equity-centred analytics which embed socio-economic and demographic data into planning tools to ensure fair distribution of urban resources. At the same time, the expansion of urban data systems brings ethical considerations to the forefront for transparent and community-centred data governance.Finally, the success of these initiatives depends not only on technological capacity but on human potential. This means, cities must invest in training professionals who possess both analytical expertise and an understanding of civic values.As urban systems grow in complexity and interdependence, this research topic reinforces the idea that data analytics, if guided by principles of ethics, inclusion, and accountability, has the capacity to serve as a transformative lever for sustainable city-making. We encourage researchers, city leaders, policymakers, and technologists to build upon these findings by advancing the real-world implementation of predictive models, exploring the use of generative AI in urban simulation, embedding participatory planning practices into formal governance structures, and institutionalizing frameworks that uphold data transparency and public trust.In sum, while cutting-edge technologies are vital in addressing the complex challenges of 21stcentury urban life, they are only part of the equation. The true sustainability of future cities will be shaped not just by the brilliance of their innovations, but by the boldness of their vision, the inclusivity of their planning, and the resilience of their communities. Data and analytics offer us the tools-but it is our shared values, ethical leadership, and collective commitment that will determine whether our cities become thriving hubs of opportunity for all, or mirrors of deepening inequality. The future is not something we inherit-it's something we build, together.

title: Editorial: Artificial intelligence: cultural policy, management, education, and research
abstract: The less productive corollary to opening such a window into these artistic worlds, is the way we respond when our attention is oriented towards emergent questions. These issues are regularly approached with either 'wait and see' reticence regarding the drawing of conclusions, or futurology with sufficient leeway to avoid being proven wrong. Typically, this comes with an attendant avoidance of meaningful contribution.Consequently despite there being fundamental issues at stake, researchers' interactions with industry and policy can fall into the trap of stating or at least agreeing that 'it's too early to tell' and then very quickly 'it's too late to do anything about it' (Zittrain, 2024). The reshaping of Creative and Cultural Industries globally is underway, it is thus incumbent on researchers to contribute meaningful analyses to enable stakeholders to act in an informed manner. Such actions may pertain to ongoing and uncertain engagements in legal, regulatory, and economic spheres, but the continuous nature of events should not preclude well developed positions. For instance, to make an argument in relation to technology companies' activities and power dynamics in the creative and Cultural Industries, stakeholders should be able to productively consider when 'can' implies 'ought' (Zittrain, 2017) regarding AI giants' influence on setting terms for creators' rights and remuneration, and how to articulate preferred directions.Whilst there are studies on AI and creative practice (Hunt and McKelvey, 2019;Miller, 2019;European Parliament. Directorate General for Internal Policies of the Union., 2020; Zylinska, 2020;Hageback and Hedblom, 2022; members of the Smithsonian AI & ML community, 2022; Wallace, 2023), to date there has been very little research into the impact of AI on Cultural Policy, or on Cultural Policies' impact on AI. The work on discipline specific creative AI practice is rich, however the gap in knowledge in the context of Cultural Policy limits the ability of artists, policy makers, managers and educators to support the responsible adoption, or strategic non adoption of AI technologies in the Creative and Cultural Sector.History has shown us that creative practitioners can help us identify new ways of seeing the world, define new ethical principles, critique social norms and interrogate emerging technologies in ways that generate both economic and social value. In many ways artists help us to know what questions we should be asking when it comes to thinking about the ethics of AI, but to do this important work, they need Cultural Policies, and funding ecosystems that value their contribution to making advanced technologies (in this case, AI), better for society.The value of the papers presented here equate to more than the sum of their parts and define a new area of policy studies, that of -AI and Cultural Policy, Practice and Management. This special issue makes practical analytic contributions through direct considerations and proposals for understanding across a breadth of creative fields. These articles do so by presenting evidential data drawn from embedded fieldwork by academics, policy makers and practitioners from creative hubs in the UK, China, and Europe. Such advances include grasping the lived experience of cultural workers (Frost and Vargas, 2024), examining the impact of AI technologies on both creative practice 'artwork' and the working conditions of artists' 'art work ' (Duester, 2024), developing clear frameworks to organise understandings of change drivers and mechanisms for spillover and growth from the Creative and Cultural Sector to the wider creative industries (Andrews and Hawcroft, 2024), mapping the dichotomy between sector ending or sector sustaining AI adoption practices in British TV (Connock, 2024), analysing the use of Generative AI technologies in the workflow process of design (Bertola and Rizzi, 2025), and the application of existing and emerging legal frameworks for the management of copyright in the context of AI technologies in the Cultural Heritage sector (Westenberger and Farmaki, 2025).The questions raised in these papers connect to key questions, that are fundamental to AI in the wider Creative and Cultural Industries, questions about the nature of creativity (Bassett, 2024;Gaut, 2010) and the role of data (Terras et al., 2024), but with a framing to consider the practical infrastructure arranging current activity. Potential implications of policy on AI influenced creative practice is subject to much debate, but the intersection of different domains of policy development (from management to education, labour to public institutions), as well as interrelations across regulatory regimes and markets are much more rarely considered (Noam and Buckweitz, 2024). This issue, came at the invitation of ENCATC, the European Network on Cultural Management and Policy, who commissioned the editors to consider the impact of AI technologies on the Creative and Cultural Sector. The invitation to edit this special issue followed the Keynote address by Dr. Oonagh Murphy to the 2023 ENCATC Summit in Helsinki, in which she established the pressing need for empirical research to empower policy makers to make evidence-based decisions around the use of AI technologies in the Creative and Cultural Sector. This issue's examinations of AI are informed by a wealth of disciplinary perspectives and serve as a starting point for thinking about the challenges and opportunities of AI in the Creative and Cultural Sector from an ecosystem not projects perspective. Cultural Policy is the top-level mechanism by which funding is allocated, and ecosystems are built. The papers presented in this special issue begin to fill the gap in knowledge concerning AI in the creative and cultural sector from a policy standpoint. In doing so we hope that they can also support the development of robust, innovative and applied approaches to Cultural Policy that empowers the Creative and Cultural sector in its relationship with AI technologies and those that develop them.We wish to extend a special thanks to the reviewers, leading authorities in their fields, who so kindly provided their expert insights and made this collection possible. Their hard work and dedication is invaluable.

title: Application of Deep Learning in the Digital Transformation of Urban Planning
abstract: This study demonstrates how deep learning technologies can enhance the efficiency and accuracy of urban spatial layout optimization, cultural heritage preservation, and transportation network planning. The study explores the application of deep learning in the digital transformation of urban planning, specifically focusing on Beijing’s central axis, an area rich in historical and cultural significance. By utilizing an improved DeepLabv3+ model, pixel-level classification of urban functional zones was achieved, with accuracy exceeding 90%, significantly surpassing traditional models. Furthermore, the study applied an enhanced graph attention network to analyze the spatial relationships between different regions, plots, roads, and intersections, revealing the complex interactions between urban functions and connectivity. These findings validate deep learning’s capability to accurately capture intricate spatial features, optimize urban layouts, and support data-driven decision-making. The study also underscores the importance of balancing technological innovation with cultural heritage preservation and community involvement. A strategic framework for integrating artificial intelligence and big data into smart city development is proposed, offering valuable guidance for policymakers, data scientists, and engineers. This framework contributes to the advancement of sustainable and intelligent urban environments.

title: Global accord on the integration of artificial intelligence in medical science publishing: implications of the Bletchley Declaration
abstract: This manuscript was handled by Deputy Editor, Charalambos Antoniades. Paying homage to the ground-breaking work of World War II’s cryptanalysts, Britain coordinated the ‘Bletchley Declaration’, a pivotal document designed to strengthen global collaboration on artificial intelligence (AI) safety.1 This declaration, endorsed by 28 countries and the European Union, was revealed as a culprit of the AI Safety Summit held at Bletchley Park, the very site where Alan Turing and his contemporaries pioneered the field of modern computing. Just as for the current AI Safety Summit, international cooperation was at the heart of Turing’s success, which included breaking the Enigma code by developing ground-breaking contributions of less visible, but hugely influential, polish mathematicians from Poznan—Rejewski, Różycki, and Zygalski.2 The venue stands as a monument to the ingenuity of mathematical breakthroughs that have continually propelled advancements in various scientific fields, including modern medicine. The Bletchley Declaration itself is a testament to the enduring importance of collaborative scientific endeavour, seeking to harness the full potential of AI while navigating its risks with international unity and foresight.1 The integration of AI into scientific publishing is not only imminent but is already in motion, putting medical publishing at a crucial crossroads. Concerns voiced during the summit included risks of AI tools replacing human contributions in the workforce as faster, more accurate, and efficient. Is that the future of science? At least at present, however, the flexibility, creativity, and uniqueness of human mind make us believe that human-driven scientific discovery, while hugely aided by AI tools, will continue to be at the centre of medical progress. The growth of AI tools, however, can greatly revolutionize medical science publishing. It brings promise to enhance data analysis making us quickly uncover multiple layers of complexity in medical data, accelerate research dissemination, improve content curation, and optimize accessibility.3 We experienced the efficacy of such approaches during an unprecedented discovery path to develop COVID-19 vaccines and understand health impacts of this pandemic.4 AI tools for in-depth and advanced discovery of biomarkers but also novel mechanisms of disease, may provide, at least in part, an alternative to the use of animal models and other complex biological systems.5–8 However, it becomes imperative to navigate the challenges that come with these great promises responsibly. To harness AI’s potential ethically and effectively, we must commit to principles that prioritize safety, human-centric design, trustworthiness, and responsible sharing of the outcomes. Our collective aim should be to enable utilization of AI in ways that bolster discovery, driving sustainable development and innovation. These overarching aims were clearly emphasized in the Bletchley Declaration1 and align perfectly with aims of medical research. At the same time, the ‘AI Safety Summit’ emphasized that the proliferation of AI systems in everyday life underscores the urgency of our commitment to safe AI development.1 This is especially relevant in areas that directly affect human health and wellbeing. One of the most important risks, particularly in medical publishing where accuracy is paramount, is potential for misinformation or inaccuracy that can have dire consequences.9 The call for international collaboration to address these challenges is clear in the Bletchley Declaration. We must work towards the development of transparent AI systems specifically designed for medical research and publishing purposes, whose processes and decisions can be easily explained and understood, ensuring fairness, alignment with ethical standards, and accountability. The advent of powerful general-purpose AI models termed by the Declaration as ‘frontier AI’, capable of performing a wide array of tasks, poses additional safety risks.1 The medical publishing sector must be vigilant against the misuse of AI, intentional or otherwise, and strive for alignment with human intent. Awareness of potential utility of these tools by already existing ‘paper mills’ and other groups unethically misusing available data is of paramount importance. This includes potential for AI to inadvertently contribute to issues like disinformation within the medical domain—a risk we cannot overlook. Given the inherently international nature of medical science publishing and the risks posed by AI, it is essential to commit to global cooperation to promote safety and trust in AI applications. While every journal is responsible for ensuring transparency and accuracy of their content, in the case of AI-related policies, a flexible cooperative approach, allowing for innovation while considering the risks, is necessary. It should foster common principles and codes of conduct that are sensitive to the varying legal and regulatory landscapes across different countries. Following valuable insights from the AI Safety Summit, we can clearly see that ensuring AI’s safety involves multiple stakeholders—governments, companies, and civil society—that all need to work closely with academia and AI industry. This may be particularly challenging when we consider inequalities in healthcare provision across the globe. Gaps in digitization are similarly huge between nations, making some areas of the world potentially particularly vulnerable.1 The list of absentees in the AI Safety Summit, as well as the Bletchley Declaration, is very visible and should be remedied by future proceedings. The digital divide must be bridged, and international collaboration should include a broad spectrum of partners, with policies that empower developing countries to build AI capacity.1 Frontier AI developers bear a particular responsibility for the safety of their systems. One of the most important practical conclusions of the AI Safety Summit was a call for rigorous safety testing, evaluations, and transparency in their operations, especially as they relate to potentially harmful effects. While we believe that multiple layers of safety approvals in medical sciences can ensure enforcement of this, difficulty in understanding complexity and details of some of the systems by the regulators poses challenges. The classic tools we use to bring medications and medical devices to clinical practice, including randomized clinical trials and layers of approval by regulatory authorities, may require adjustments and developments.1 Based on the Bletchley Declaration, one can propose some key general areas of development (Table 1). title: ReassembleNet: Learnable Keypoints and Diffusion for 2D Fresco Reconstruction
abstract: The task of reassembly is a significant challenge across multiple domains, including archaeology, genomics, and molecular docking, requiring the precise placement and orientation of elements to reconstruct an original structure. In this work, we address key limitations in state-of-the-art Deep Learning methods for reassembly, namely i) scalability; ii) multimodality; and iii) real-world applicability: beyond square or simple geometric shapes, realistic and complex erosion, or other real-world problems. We propose ReassembleNet, a method that reduces complexity by representing each input piece as a set of contour keypoints and learning to select the most informative ones by Graph Neural Networks pooling inspired techniques. ReassembleNet effectively lowers computational complexity while enabling the integration of features from multiple modalities, including both geometric and texture data. Further enhanced through pretraining on a semi-synthetic dataset. We then apply diffusion-based pose estimation to recover the original structure. We improve on prior methods by 57% and 87% for RMSE Rotation and Translation, respectively.

title: Federated Data Modelling for Heritage Building Performance Management
abstract: The fragmentation of knowledge across multiple sources and players, coupled with limited access to information, is one of the main challenges for the performance-based management of heritage buildings. Despite recent research efforts in the field of Heritage Building Information Modelling (HBIM), this technology alone is insufficient for managing the variety of data related to building performance and is challenging for stakeholders without digital expertise to adopt. These limitations, along with advancements in knowledge technologies, have led to the emergence of federated data modelling approaches as a core strategy for managing the complexity of buildings’ operational information. To address data fragmentation, this research proposes a methodology for linking heterogeneous data on historic building performance. The approach structures heterogeneous data, gathered from multiple sources—HBIM models, sensors, and energy bills—into knowledge graphs that enable semantic integration, cross-domain queries and support interactive visualisation. As part of the BeTwin research project, the methodology is validated through its application to a case study in the Appia Antica Archaeological Park (Rome, Italy).

title: Ethical Considerations for <scp>MRI</scp> Research in Human Subjects in the Era of Precision Medicine
abstract: In the field of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), the involvement of human subjects is an essential part of research investigations, technology development, and patient care. High-definition anatomical, physiological, functional, and molecular information offered by MRI is increasingly sought after in scientific discovery and precision medicine. Furthermore, the latest developments in translational and clinical research, including MRI-guided interventions and artificial intelligence-based algorithms, rely on the wealth of MRI data generated from studies on patients. As we continue to advance MRI technology to empower research and clinical care, the recent shift to an era of precision medicine must be examined in the context of the relevant ethics when involving human subjects in research studies. The opening plenary session on “Moral & Ethical Issues in MRI Research” at the 2023 annual meeting of the International Society for Magnetic Resonance in Medicine (ISMRM) brought several important issues to the forefront for the community to consider. Here, we highlight key points from the session within the framework of the Belmont Report introduced 45 years ago, specifically the importance of Respect for Persons, Beneficence, and Justice. In the modern era, investigators must consider a broad range of characteristics, including biological variables, socio economic status, cultural heritage, and life experience. The early years after adoption of the Belmont Report and other guidelines for research using human subjects, such as guiding principles for ethical research by the U.S. National Institutes of Health Clinical Center,1 were focused on establishing regulations for monitoring safety, rights, and well-being of human subjects in research. More recently, increased emphasis has been placed on the validity and quality of scientific research, including the rigor of the approaches taken, reproducibility of data, and quality of unbiased study design. A key consideration for precision medicine is the scope of inclusion for research cohorts to encompass diverse health conditions and populations. For example, it is disturbing to realize women are still underrepresented in acute coronary syndrome trials with a low ratio of participation to prevalence of 0.6,2 which may be responsible, in part, for the wide differences in healthcare outcomes. As many diseases, including cancer and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease, are highly heterogeneous, recruiting a diverse set of subjects to capture within and between subject variability is critical for validating novel technologies.3 Furthermore, epigenetic research has shown disparities in healthcare conditions and long-term environmental and socioeconomic effects can alter biological and genetic traits of healthy individuals and patients.4 Using existing datasets for developing algorithms for artificial intelligence that do not take into consideration a wide breadth of factors can result in biased and ungeneralizable results, even when the same experimental conditions are utilized.5 Understanding individual variability and incorporating thoughtful approaches to design human subject studies are particularly relevant in clinical trial design and assessment of drug efficacy as the scientific community moves toward more individualized, adaptive trial designs, and personalized medicine practices. Over representing vulnerable or specific groups is one option to address the apparent bias in existing cohorts and recruitment. Importantly, developments in MRI technology continue to enable more inclusive and diverse human subject cohorts. A notable example is the rapid technical advances to image infants and underserved populations, as most recently demonstrated by the development of portable and low-field MRI scanners.6 With the goal of generating beneficial and broadly translatable results, the plenary session also highlighted the importance of MRI safety and, more broadly, beneficence of our research to both current and future patients. There is a clear benefit in incorporating input from both MRI and non-MRI experts to ensure appropriate study design, safety of volunteers and patients in clinical trials, and data interpretation. As we develop cutting-edge methodologies using healthy volunteers for eventual clinical applications in patients, there is an important balance between relentlessly pursuing innovation and carefully assessing the risk to the subjects, particularly those with unique health or physical conditions introduced by recruiting a more diverse and heterogeneous study population. The potential safety concerns from powerful new technology must be carefully managed. The ISMRM community has established an excellent track record in assessing and mitigating the risks involved in new and advanced technologies developed in the field.7 Our continued responsibility is particularly crucial as inclusion criteria are expanded to include more diverse study populations and data sources become more open. Data sharing among scientific communities in different fields is essential to maximize the benefits and improve outcomes of human subject studies, as is unbiased testing and validation of new findings and technologies. The push toward more open science, however, also imposes challenges for data safety management.8 The delicate balance between open science and protecting the individual right to privacy is a key topic of consideration for our global MRI community. Federated learning is a potential approach for improved security, where machine learning is performed at local sites using single MRI datasets and updated neural network weights are then shared between sites. The number of clinical trials that incorporate and implement MRI methods continues to increase globally.9 International collaborations offer opportunities for broadening access to geographically, ethnically, and socioeconomically diverse populations that are critical for democratizing and globalizing MRI technology. While different regions and countries may, and should, have their own organizations and agencies that develop guidelines for research in human subjects, it is important to recognize and respect the cultural and regulatory differences before reaching a consensus for establishing fundamental principles and universal standards.10 Without acceptable global systems and policies in place, a basic understanding and good practice of ethical research in human subjects, along with the unwavering integrity held by each investigator, are the foundation for formulating and developing cross-border collaborations. ISMRM, as a scientific community of investigators in this field, is well-poised to play a prominent role in educating, promoting, and facilitating research in human subjects performed with the utmost ethical standards, highlighting the continued relevance of the Belmont Report nearly half a century later.

title: Climate Change and Inequality in the Ancient Mediterranean: A Scoping Review
abstract: (1) Background: Climate change and inequality are topics of major interest in Mediterranean Archaeology. However, comparatively less attention has been dedicated to how these themes are interlinked in the literature. No scoping review has ever addressed this issue. This study aims to identify major research trends on inequality and climate change in the Mediterranean c. 4000 BC–AD 500. It also pinpoints current research gaps on the topic and nascent areas of enquiry. (2) Method: We performed a scoping review on JSTOR, Scopus, Google Scholar and PubMed in December 2025–January 2026. A modified version of the PRISMA-ScR protocol was followed. We sampled journal articles, book chapters, edited volumes and monographs published between 2015 and 2025 which matched the search and inclusion criteria. Additional searches were done on Google Scholar in February 2026 to expand upon emerging research trends relevant to our topic but largely absent from the scoping review. We manually extracted, charted, analysed and synthesised the data. (3) Results: A total of 154 studies were eligible for the scoping review. We identified six research trends prominent in the sampled literature: 1. the rise and fall of world systems, macroscale causal links, and collapse research; 2. inequality, subalternity, and marginality; 3. agriculture, crops, and diet; 4. natural resource management, and water supply; 5. epistemology and methodology; and 6. natural archives and climate proxy datasets. We also recognised the following research gaps or topics that were comparatively less addressed: collapse research applied to the microscale level and marginalised communities; isotope analysis applied to both climate change and inequality in the same study; biomedical approaches applied to both climate change and inequality in the same study; social marginality as a complex construct in human–climate interactions; and the environmental and climate dimensions of the early Roman expansion, especially regarding marginality and the microscale. Finally, we identified artificial intelligence (AI), Big Data, environmental and climate activism, and the perception of climate hazards by subaltern communities as nascent topics of interest that might rise to prominence in the future. (4) Conclusions: We identified major research trends and gaps on climate change and inequality in the ancient Mediterranean in literature published 2015–2025. We also recognised nascent or unexplored topics. The review is intended as a benchmark for developing novel research on the cutting-edge of Mediterranean Archaeology.

title: Surveillance in Higher Education
abstract: Summary Surveillance capacities and practices in the higher education (HE) sector are expanding rapidly. Students and staff—academic and professional—are monitored using a range of technologies and for a variety of purposes. There are good reasons to explore how and why these practices are becoming increasingly normalized, and to challenge this normalization. There is a growing body of work relating to surveillance in HE, with distinctive pre- and post-COVID-19 pandemic concerns relating to the switch to remote and hybrid work and study. New questions are also arising in relation to the development of generative artificial intelligence and its embrace as a technology to support learning, teaching, and research. Existing research into surveillance capacities and practices in HE emphasizes some of the different ways in which trust is being undermined. A new “disclosive archaeology” analyzes how surveillant technologies embed and enact particular discourses and thus create new tensions within and challenges for the sector. In particular, it highlights the risks that surveillant practices pose for academic cultures, including dangers of exacerbating inequalities, entrenching extractive data practices, and distorting the basis of collegial and cooperative knowledge generation that underpins both research and teaching.

title: How to problematize a border, or: some ongoing notes on transient methodologies
abstract: In this paper I rehearse a method for studying media that is engaged by what I am calling a transient methodology. This work with “transients“ emerges as much as an analytical tool as it does as a material engagement, in direct connection with my encounter with a GDR-era synthesizer prototype, the Subharchord I/II, and its use of a specific audio filter design which is found again only forty years later as a building block for most state-of-the-art speech recognition algorithms. I am particularly interested in one such algorithm, namely the so-called “Dialect Recognition Software”, a proprietary machine learning solution in use since 2017 by the German Office for Migration and Refugees in cases of undocumented asylum seekers in the country. By bringing these two stories closer and mobilizing them through the work of transients – a concept that works in sound as much as it does in movement – I seek to activate an experimental, speculative media archaeology that focuses on the haptics of listening. Transient methodologies, I argue, offer the potential to critically listen to these two technologies together while at the same time slowing them down for critical inquiry and analysis.

title: Photogrammetry of selected skeletal trauma from Iron and Viking-Age Scandinavia: a BODY-POLITICS 3D-model dataset
abstract: Overview These are the 3D models generated for the individuals A1860, X2753 and 4278-PF (3 individuals) in the formats of .PLY with texture and .OBJ with texture. The 3D models (secondary data) were generated with the photogrammetric software Agisoft Metashape by Dr Vasiliki Louka using image files (primary data) captured by Dr Emma Tollefsen from the physical skeletal remains. The models have been uploaded as .zip and can be viewed by using a 3D viewer or further imported to open-access sofwtare such as Blender. Dr Vasiliki Louka accessed the software Agisoft Metashapte at the ULAS (University of Leicester Archaeological Services) facilities at the University of Leicester. The images were imported to the software and were processed in order to generater a point cloud. The cloud was further processed to increase accuracy and reduce unecessary points by utilising the settings provided by the Agisoft Metashape user interface. Finally, the 3D meshes were produced and the texture was applied to create the final 3D model. Screenshot of the corresponding models appear in the relevant manuscript. About photogrammetry "Photogrammetry is the science and technology of obtaining information about the physical environment from images, with a focus on applications in surveying, mapping and high-precision metrology (Schindler and Förstner 2021)". In essence, photogrammetry is the method through which 2D data from image sources (e.g., photography, video) are transformed to generate 3D by being imported in a photogrammetric software. For these models, the photographs were taken with 50%+ overlap with each other using a Canon EOS 2000D DSLR and a tripod. The selected remains were mounted on a turntable in front of a white backdrop. Once obtained, the images were imported to Agisoft Metashape. The quality of the images was calculated while images with suboptimal quality (blurred, over- or underexposed) were removed. The remaining images were aligned to obtain the initial sparse cloud which was further processed to remove unecessary points and areas (e.g., the background). The final mesh was generated afterwards and then texture was applied to produce the finished, textured 3D model. The operational system for photogrammetry was a HP Z4 G4 Workstation (x64-based PC), with Intel(R) Core(TM), i9-7900X CPU @ 3.30Mhz (10 Core(s), 20 Logical Processor(s)). Acknowledgements We would like to thank the staff from University of Leicester Archaeological Services for granting access to the facilities and permitting use of the software Agisoft Metashape. title: MillefioriAnalyzer: Machine Learning, Computer Vision and Visual Analytics for Provenance Research of Ancient Roman Artefacts
abstract: In this position paper, we explore ways to digitally support provenance research of ancient Roman artefacts decorated with millefiori. In particular, we discuss experiments applying visual analytics, computer vision and machine learning approaches to analyze the relations between images of individual millefiori slices called florets. We start by applying automatic image analysis approaches to the florets and discover that image quality and the small overall number of images pose serious challenges to these approaches. To address these challenges, we bring human intuition and pattern recognition abilities back into the analysis loop by developing and employing visual analytics techniques. We achieve a convenient analysis workflow for the archaeologists by integrating all approaches into a single interactive software tool which we call MillefioriAnalyzer. The software is tailored to fit the needs of the archaeological application case and links the automatic image analysis approaches with the interactive visual analytics views. As appropriate for a research software, MillefioriAnalyzer is open-source and publicly available. First results include an automatic approximate ordering of florets and a visual analytics module improving upon the current manual image layout for further analytic reasoning.

title: Code Word Cloud in Franz Kafka’s “Beim Bau der Chinesischen Mauer” [“The Great Wall of China”]
abstract: Amidst the centenary reflections on Franz Kafka’s legacy, this article explores his work’s ongoing resonance with the digital age, particularly through the lens of generative AI and cloud computation. Anchored in a close reading of Kafka’s “Beim Bau der chinesischen Mauer”, this study interrogates how the spatial and temporal codes embedded in the narrative parallel the architectures of contemporary diffusion systems at the heart of AI models. Engaging with critical theory, media archaeology, and AI discourse, this article argues that the rise of large language models not only commodifies language but also recasts Kafka’s allegorical critiques of bureaucratic opacity and imperial command structures within a digital framework. The analysis leverages concepts like Kittler’s code, Benjamin’s figural cloud, and Hamacher’s linguistic dissemblance to position Kafka’s parables as proto-critical tools for examining AI’s black-box nature. Ultimately, the piece contends that Kafka’s text is less a metaphor for our technological present than a mirror reflecting the epistemological crises engendered by the collapse of semantic transparency in the era of algorithmic communication. This reframing invites a rethinking of how narrative, code, and digital architectures intersect, complicating our assumptions about clarity, control, and the digital regimes shaping contemporary culture.

title: Conference Report on Evolang 11
abstract: The 11th International Conference on the Evolution of Language (Evolang 11) was hosted at the Lavin-Bernick Center for University Life at Tulane University in New Orleans, LA, USA, from 21 March to 24 March 2016. The University of Southern Mississippi organised the conference, with Heidi Lyn as Chair of the local organising committee. Over 200 delegates gathered for this second American Evolang, and were treated not only to a wide range of current research in language origins and evolution, but also to local ‘NOLA’ food and culture as well. Evolang hosted a reception at Mardi Gras World—a stylised warehouse storing numerous Mardi Gras floats and costumes, where guests were serenaded with a brass band and committee members threw beads into the amused, cocktail-sipping crowd. The conference banquet was held at the colonial-era-style Audubon Tea Room with live jazz and a swing dancing lesson led by Thom Scott-Phillips. Post-conference events included a ghost tour, swamp tours, and a plantation tour. This was the 20th anniversary of the very first Evolang, held in Edinburgh in 1996, and saw the release of the first issue of the Journal of Language Evolution . With a 20-year history, it is hardly surprising that there has been a strong ‘self-reflective’ tendency at recent Evolang conferences, as witnessed, for example, in the ‘Perspectives on Evolang’ section in the proceedings of Evolang 10 (Cartmill et al. 2014) , as well as in some of the contributions in the first issue of JoLE ( Dediu and de Boer 2016 ; Hammarström 2016 ). Something that is repeatedly mentioned in these publications is the observation that ‘work on language evolution has become much more rigorous: we are discovering methods by which questions we could formerly only speculate about can now be investigated empirically’ ( de Boer 2014 ). These ‘self-reflective’ tendencies were also exemplified by two papers that took an empirical outlook on language evolution research. Wacewicz, Zywiczynski, and Jasinski investigated to what extent and in what way introductory textbooks featured the subject of language evolution, whereas Bergmann and Dale used advanced quantitative methods for a data-driven analysis of abstracts from the past Evolang conferences from 2006 to 2014. Drawing on a Latent Dirichlet Allocation Algorithm, Bergmann and Dale identified twenty major topics, whereby each topic consists of a distribution of semantically related words. These topics were then clustered using a community detection algorithm, yielding a network of correlated topics that roughly mirrors the variety of subfields represented at Evolang, which offered Evolang attendees a charming way to reflect on how the field has grown to its current state of multiple branching research areas. The highly interdisciplinary character of the field was reflected in the choice of plenary speakers. Marine biologist Vincent Janik (University of St Andrews) talked about the evolution of complexity in the calls of captive grey seals and dolphins. Joan Bybee (University of New Mexico), a historical linguist, gave a very broad overview of mechanisms of language change, arguing that the same processes that can be observed in the traceable history of human languages have been in play at the very beginnings of language. Evolutionary anthropologist Dean Falk (Florida State University) proposed an ‘evo-devo’ hypothesis according to which the relationship between human infants and caregivers played a key role in the selection for ‘parentese’ and, eventually, grammatical language. Ljiljana Progovac (Wayne State University), a minimalist syntactician, proposed a linguistic reconstruction of the earliest stages of grammar and discussed its implications regarding the plausibility of different scenarios of language evolution. Erich Jarvis (Duke University) showed how brain regions for motor control are integrated into the song system for vocal learning birds, and fervently advocated for the inclusion of other non-human, non-primate species as models of language evolution. In addition, Evolang 11 featured two ‘discussion plenaries’, the aim of which were to spark debate not only between the debating plenary speakers but also among the conference-goers. The first discussion plenary was dedicated to language localisation in the brain. Although at first Sharon Thompson-Schill and Evelina Fedorenko claimed that they actually had very little to disagree about, in the rebuttals to each other's talks it became apparent that Thompson-Schill prefers a more domain-general view of language in the brain than does Fedorenko. Both strongly agreed, however, on the importance of new modelling of neural networks and not just focusing on localised regions. The second discussion plenary pitted Thom Scott-Phillips and Richard Moore in a friendly but animated debate concerning the nature of the development of intentional communication. The debate was a re-enactment of their series of papers responding to one another (e.g. Moore 2016 ; Scott-Phillips 2016 ), and did well to highlight this ongoing philosophical disagreement to a wider audience. Two later talks by Heidi Lyn and Erica Cartmill harked back to this debate and were able to show the relevance of how we discuss intentionality in non-human communication. This was the first time the conference included talks in this discussion format and the response was positive. One of the theoretical take-home messages of Evolang 11 was that the traditional picture of Broca's and Wernicke's areas is simply not enough to fully account for linguistic activity. During the workshop on The Evolution of Speech (Fitch, de Boer and Nishimura), it was stressed that there is no ‘key factor’ promoting speech evolution, but rather a set of factors and elements intervening at the same time. One factor would be the motor neurons projected to the laryngeal muscles, also discussed during Eric Jarvis' talk, where he stressed the role played by basal ganglia in species he called ‘vocal learners’ (including humans, elephants, bats, seals, and humming birds, among others). In parallel, Joana Rosselló incorporated this point in her talk about vocal learning, putting forth a hypothesis in which language is rooted in a vocal learning system where human words stand apart from alarm calls or bird song due to encoded meaning. Ackerman and Ziegler also stressed the role of basal ganglia in language, providing important data from neurology and clinical linguistics. Evelina Fedorenko also rightly pointed out that while a lot of effort goes into understanding the production of language, the sheer memory upon which language relies is highly underappreciated. In contrast to Evolang 9 in Kyoto, where mirror neurons were discussed a number of times, talks presented at Evolang 11 on theoretical linguistics, neurology, and clinical studies favoured a cortical–subcortical complex network. If this paradigm holds, it raises an important question for language evolution theory: what happened in the case of hominins with which modern humans interbred with multiple times ( Vernot et al. 2016 ), such as Neanderthals and Denisovans? Were they vocal learners too? The theoretical debate on Neanderthal language was nearly absent at this conference, after more intense discussion during past years (e.g. Johansson 2013a , b ; Barceló-Coblijn and Benítez-Burraco 2013 ); in fact, discussion of archaeological and palaeoanthropological topics were almost completely lacking, save for Dean Falk’s plenary discussion of ‘parentese’, which was situated in human evolution since the last common ancestor, and an experimental approach to identify intentionality in stone tools by Cory Cuthbertson. These theoretical and empirical advances surely foster new comments and considerations in the complex study of language evolution in our species’ ancestry. Approaches like Olga Vasileva’s, who along with others such as Marieke Woensdregt et al. incorporated the ability of mentalising as an important topic to language evolution studies. They imported interesting concepts from biological theory into the analysis of clinical data related to language, which is crucial for a better understanding of how theoretical concepts and data from biology could shed light onto language evolution studies. Other researchers, in addition to Erich Jarvis, were vocal about the need to look further than primates in comparative studies. This was not merely a gripe against primatologists, but rather a suggestion for those who reference animal papers when backing up their theories to include a wider taxonomic range. Interestingly, much of the emphasis was on the use in looking at bird models of language evolution. However, looking at the papers presented, twelve were given on primates and eight were given on birds—not such a large difference. The glaring gap in study species was not primates or birds, but all other animal species, which starred in only four of the presentations. One of these presentations was Vincent Janik’s plenary on marine mammals, and the three remaining papers were on bottlenose dolphins, mongooses, and dogs (mentioned alongside primate research by Heidi Lyn). It is encouraging to see more animal communication studies at Evolang, and in future we should encourage researchers who work on more diverse species. As Scott-Phillips and Kirby (2010 : 412) point out, the term ‘evolution of language’ can refer both to the evolution of the biological capacity for language and to the subsequent cultural evolution of language. Experimental studies with human subjects trained on artificial languages have proven a highly insightful way of studying the latter process. In particular, the Iterated Learning (IL) paradigm ( Kirby et al. 2008 ) has become highly influential, and papers using the IL method were well represented at this year's Evolang. In fact, ‘Iterated Learning’ occupies rank three of the most chosen keywords in the online proceedings, only surpassed by ‘cultural evolution’ and ‘gesture’. One paper (Motamedi et al.) 1 The abstracts and full papers for all conference talks mentioned in this report can be found in the conference proceedings ( Roberts et al. 2016 ) ‘Cumulative culture’ is one of the buzzwords in language evolution research, and it popped up at Evolang in an unexpected way, in a talk by Adriano Lameira about orangutan vocalisations. Of course, natural languages play an equally important role in assessing patterns of cultural evolution to experimental models. Evolang 11 showed once again that large-scale correlational studies enjoy growing popularity in the Evolang community while at the same time, in the wake of cautionary papers like Roberts and Winters (2013) , becoming ever more rigid methodologically. Christian Bentz used entropy measures to estimate the complexity of 646 languages from word frequency distributions in parallel text samples, identifying a geo-spatial pattern around the equator he refers to as ‘the low-complexity belt’. As a tentative explanation for this finding, he suggests that large-scale prehistoric language contact might have taken place in this geographical area. Berdicevskis and Eckhoff, by contrast, only focused on one language family, namely the Slavic languages, to show that the functionality (non-redundancy) of morphological features can serve as a predictor of the survivability of those features in the course of language change. Probably the largest sample of different languages was used by Jaeger and Wichmann. Drawing on vocabulary lists from more than 6,000 languages, they computed a phylogenetic language tree covering all continents and language families using methods from computational biology. Evolang 11 continued the high quality of previous Evolang conferences and offered a broad variety of exciting new insights from all areas of language evolution research. Many excellent papers were presented by young researchers, so it was not easy for the Hurford prize committee to determine the winner of this year's award for the best paper presented by a PhD student. Five runners-up (as compared to two at Evolang 10) received honourable mentions and an Evolang mug, but the actual award went to Michelle Spierings for her paper on rule learning in zebra finches, co-authored with Carel ten Cate. The prize for the best poster went to Andreas Baumann, Christina Prömer, Kamil Kazmierski, and Nikolaus Ritt, who presented a computational model of the dynamics of compositional markers. In addition, Evolang 11 introduced some changes that mostly met with approval at the general meeting. There was a broad consensus that the newly established double-blind peer review contributes to ensure the high quality of presentations at Evolang and that it demonstrably led to a fairer selection process (see also Roberts, this volume). The opinions concerning the new publication format of the proceedings ( Roberts et al. 2016 ) were somewhat more controversial: While some missed the printed books, many others welcomed the decision to make this year's proceedings available online open-access under a creative commons licence, with the option to include supplementary materials. In addition to the individual papers, which can be accessed via the online interface at http://evolang.org/neworleans , the proceedings can now also be downloaded as a collective volume with running page numbers at http://dx.doi.org/10.17617/2.2248195 . The next Evolang conference will return to Europe and will take place in Toruń, Poland. At the closing session, Przemyslaw Zywiczynski and Slawomir Wacewicz sparked participants' anticipation with a teaser presentation on the manifold merits of Toruń, city of Copernicus and gingerbread. As old friends and colleagues and new acquaintances left each other’s company, Evolang’s warm and diverse community separated ways for another two-year wait until the next conference meeting.
